author: @ETechTreasures
text: Pretty solid breakdown in this video. As a Tesla Model Y owner, I’m always weighing space versus utility, and the WildbearX looks like it would fit in the trunk without hogging too much room. That’s honestly one of my main concerns with coolers since road trips already eat up a lot of cargo space. Nice to see something that seems more compact but still holds up decently well.

author: @amanaly09
text: I actually bought my WildbearX off their Kickstarter campaign a while back after first spotting an ad on Google. A buddy of mine was already using it and swore by it, so that helped push me over the edge. It’s been really solid for day trips and small gatherings, though I’ll admit a few of the compartments feel a little smaller than I expected. Still, I’ve been surprised by how well it holds ice considering the size—it easily lasted us through a full day at the lake in the heat.

author: @explorewithwilliaam
text: @amanaly09  Been using the WildbearX mostly for camping and fishing trips, and I’d say it punches above its weight for a smaller cooler. I’ve had it keep drinks cold well into the next morning, which is impressive given that it doesn’t look like a massive ice chest. It’s also tough enough to toss in the back of the truck without worrying about scratches or dings. For anyone who does weekend outdoors stuff, it’s a nice mix of durability and portability.

author: @NatureEssentialsNE
text: @explorewithwilliaam  For those of you who’ve actually used the WildbearX—how does the ice retention compare to some of the bigger-name coolers out there (like Yeti or RTIC)? I get that it’s more compact, but I’m curious if the insulation performance really stacks up in practice. Does it hold ice for multiple days, or is it more of a one-day-use type of cooler?

author: @meryOdays
text: @NatureEssentialsNE  Good question. From my experience, it doesn’t quite match the multi-day ice life of something like a big Yeti—those are built like tanks and take up way more space. The WildbearX is more of a “one full day, maybe a little into the next morning” kind of cooler if you pack it smart. For me that tradeoff works, because I’d rather save trunk space and have something easier to carry. If you’re planning longer off-grid trips, you’d probably want a bigger unit, but for day trips or weekend drives it holds up really well.

Marques has genuine influence, so it doesn't make sense to have "influencers" in quotations. How do you know their level of awareness to the average lifestyle? It's a starter EV because it is among the cheaper EVs that exist. I could be uninformed, but I've never heard of an electric car that costs even near $1,000,000. Again, nothing shown or mentioned in this video costs close to $1,000,000.

     You're misunderstanding the word "starter", in this case it means the Model 3 is a good entry point into EV ownership. The Tesla Model 3 is one of the most accessible EVs on the market. It's got great performance, solid range, and lots of tech and features c͟o͟m͟p͟a͟r͟e͟d͟ to any other EV in the same price range. Combined, this makes the Tesla Model 3 a great option for someone entering the EV category. This is what "starter" means in this context. You can get a Model 3 for around $35,000 from Tesla, which is agreeably not cheap. Relatively speaking, however, it is somewhat cheap. Can you think of another EV which offers the same things for the same price? No, you can't, because it doesn't exist.

     Calling it a "starter" car isn't a classist remark, as if people should be starting with a Model 3, then be moving to something more expensive; it's a relative term to compare it to other EVs in it's class.

text: Completely agree with this content. author: @mandelm2001
text:
Most people don’t appreciate all the features that come with even the cheapest Tesla, and how easy it is to upgrade. Because it is software based Tesla can add new features as needed.

I had a Genesis, which is a Hyundai Mercedes copy. It came with auto folding outside mirrors that tilt down when you reverse, adaptive cruise control, heated and cooled seats, easy entry, power seats and windows, and a premium sound system. It had Apple Car Play, but it was wired. Unfortunately the nav software was provided by a third party so to upgrade I had to research how to get it, pay $125, download to a flash drive, and then plug the flash drive into the dash.

Every Tesla has all those features and wireless charging, plus features like dog and sentry mode, auto blinker shutoff after lane change, blind spot camera views and now red alert, green light alert at stop lights, and literally thousands more. All provided by a software update in the middle of the night.

This update process has no peer in the auto industry. Nobody talks about it in EV car reviews though, it needs a lot more visibility.

author: @mandelm2001
text:
Curious about the term “Starter EV”. Do you mean entry level or standard bearer? 

A premium car with ambient lighting, back seat video, and Tesla software is now the standard for EVs around the world. I have the standard range and it’s all anyone needs, and it starts at $38K now with no incentives. That’s well below the average cost of all new cars. The value prop is stunning.

Used Teslas can be had for under $30K. Even without the new lower cost car, the current lineup is very competitive with ICE cars.

author: @mandelm2001
text:
Yeah Teslas are different. The sparse interior is a big change. However after driving one for a while you learn to love all the room, flat floor so no drivetrain hump, and ultra convenience. I set all features to auto. Headlights turn on when needed, and brights automatically turn on and off when needed. A drivers profile has all settings like seat and steering wheel position, easy entry mode, mirrors, climate, wipers, and driving mode, and each driver has a profile.

From your phone app you can precondition your car before driving so it’s all warmed up and ready to go. The car unlocks as you approach and locks when you leave the car.

I can open the tailgate with my watch app.

All commands like setting temp and fan speed, picking a song to play on Spotify, or changing the volume of the music can be done with voice commands.

It’s all different, and much better.

author: @gottagowork
text:
Color is great, hell, I'll even go amazing on this one. Form is great. I've never been a fan of Tesla interior, and removing stocks and regular car cockpit/functions is just absolutely horrible design (I voted against Volvo EX-30 for same reason). But I absolutely despise Musk, what he has chosen to represent, and extremely bad business practices, so I never "fell for it" (despite looking good with performance to match). Those biased opinions aside, my warnings and negatives comes mostly from Tesla owners who have had theirs for a while and their experience with it as a brand. 

Just as suspected, while making a good *looking* EV when the rest produced abominations early on (now fully addressed), they had no expertise as an auto maker. Meaning quality would suffer. And referring to other videos by experienced owners, quality have been a severe issue. And I'm not talking about "quality" on a brand new vehicle, but quality down the line after having used it for a few years. Brand new "quality" doesn't mean anything, anyone should be able to get this right.

So with those in mind, I wouldn't recommend Tesla at all, for anyone. If there was anything I'd look up before a purchase from any brand, it would be looking up manufacturers history wrt bad consumer practices. If they force you to buy a whole assembly worth $4000 (self steering unit, happens to be Hyundai in this case, but many car manufacturers are extremely customer hostile these days - maybe all of them?) when it's a $140 part in that assembly that is broken and can easily be replaced - that's when you should just put them on the no-go list.

author: @johnnyanko6051
text:
I had a very scary experience with the new model 3 last weekend. I got an extended test drive during the whole weekend, so I tested it vigorously. I found myself constantly looking down before pressing the turn signal buttons before exiting roundabouts, particularly the smaller ones. Otherwise, it's impossible to hit the correct button, and even then it's too easy to hit the wrong one. I found that I lost track of my surroundings and became way too distracted at times because of this. 
One time I almost hit a pedestrian when exiting a roundabout. I was too focused on finding the button to press. I only looked down for a few seconds, but that was enough. When I looked up, a pedestrian was suddenly right in front of me and I had to slam on the brakes. Other cars behind me had to do the same and nearly hit me from behind. That really scared me. I've been driving for 20 years, and I've never been close to running over anyone before. I think these buttons are dangerous and shouldn't be legal. it's the only thing keeping me from buying one. I loved so many of the upgrades, so this was a real shame. I really liked the car, but I'm not sure I would ever be comfortable using this.
I live in the EU by the way, and we have roundabouts everywhere. It's probably not much of an issue in the US though.

text:
2:46 - How did they get away with NO visible lights on the body of the car while the trunk is open? 
Lights MUST ALWAYS be visible to oncoming traffic even while the trunk is open. This is a safety requirement by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) on ALL vehicles. e.g. If you are parked on the side of the road (especially at night) and your trunk is open because you are loading stuff, oncoming vehicles NEED to see you. They can't see you if the Tail Light is up in the air. This why manufactures always split the lights if the light is attached onto a moving part (trunk) of the vehicle. 
Tesla ignored this this. Expect a safety recall soon.

text: @Eman1900O I’ve kept each of my previous cars about 8 years or so, and my intention with my Model 3 is—or wasn’t—any different. But the 2024 Highland refresh addresses several annoyances and makes what was already an excellent car more nearly perfect, so it’s tempting to upgrade. I probably won’t, because it’s financially stupid, but it’s tempting. And it’s not like the old car would get thrown in the garbage. It’s in excellent shape and would be a great car for someone in the used EV market. I hear complaints all the time about how there aren’t enough good used EVs in the market yet for people wanting to get an EV, so, while selling my three-year-old Model 3 would be financially stupid for me, it would be good for someone else and for society as a whole, so why give me or anyone else a bad time about that?

author: @conradce
text: @Eman1900O I’ve kept each of my last three cars about eight years or so, and that was my original intention with my Model 3 when I bought it three years ago. But the improvements they’ve made are very tempting. I probably won’t buy it because it isn’t a very financially smart thing to do. But if I do, why the criticism? It’s not like the old one would be going to the scrap heap. It’s in excellent shape and would get sold, helping someone else get into an EV at a more affordable price point. I’ve read articles lamenting that there aren’t enough good used EVs out there yet, so even though upgrading to the new one might be stupid for me to do, it’s maybe a good thing to do overall.

author: @Jo_Obst
text: My partner has had a 2024 Model 3 as a company car for 6 weeks now, and we love it. As MKBHD said, it‘s the perfect EV for beginners, even for me as a stick shift enthusiast, just so quiet and comfortable, yet quick. There is just one problem, and it‘s not the missing stalks: with the facelift, Tesla got rid of the dedicated parking sensors and also the rain sensor. The latter is a big problem, because the variable wiper interval just doesn‘t work anymore. The car almost never notices rain, and we have to use the button on the steering wheel repeatedly, except in some cases when we drive behind another car. The lighter the color of the car in front of us, the more „rain“ the car „sees“. In a queue behind a white truck, the wiper goes berserk, even in a light drizzle.

author: @johnfranklin6394
text:
Just had a test drive. First  Tesla I have ever driven, after testing many other EVs. 

I drive an ICE BMW, so never owned an EV.

This Tesla is by far the best EV I have tested. It simply blows the others away that I have tested, and that includes the BMW i4 and iX1, Audi Q4 e-tron, Polestar 2, Volvo XC40 Recharge, Nissan Ariya, Smart #1 and Toyota bz4x.

I tested the entry level single motor car. To be honest, it was more than quick enough for me, faster than my 265hp BMW.

The ride was superb on the potholed roads of Stockport in the UK. It was super quiet inside, with far less tyre roar compared to my BMW.

I also liked the accurate and responsive steering, it gave me total confidence over control and placement of the car in multilane lane traffic.

As for the lack of steering wheel stalks, that took maybe two minutes to get used to. While the steering wheel mounted controls for indicators and wipers are unconventional by traditional car standards, I quickly found them very intuitive.

So, as I expected, the Tesla Model 3 is clearly the best EV in my price range. It is simply next level compared to offerings from the “heritage” brands out there.

author: @reidconti
text:
Just drove a RWD one at Fremont. Coming from our 2018 RWD, it's definitely a big upgrade in most departments. We don't have the double-glazed glass or extra sound deadening that the 2020s got, nor do we have eco tires anymore, so it's hard for me to say how much of the improvement is from  2020 vs 2024 updates. But it's just INCREDIBLY solid and quiet. I was super impressed. I like the interior improvements and tweaks a lot, too. The new wheel, especially being heated, is awesome. I found it odd that MKB was so outspoken about the stereo, and it being a "mini Model S". The stereo on our 3 punches WAY above its weight for the era. My father has a 2017 S and the stereo is *awful*. I'm sure the S got a much better system over the years, but the 3 was way better than the S when it was released.

On the downside, the lack of stalks. Sorry, that's a deal-breaker for me. Even the stalks on our 3 (and on my X5) that don't stay where you put them, are bad. BMW came to their senses and went back to stateful stalks, but Tesla learned the wrong lesson. The swipe-to-drive is okay but awkward, again, a downgrade.
On the styling front, while I like the new headlights and the leading edge of the new bumper, the rest of the front bumper is a bland downgrade. The loss of the lower lamps and foglights and the scallops in front of the front wheels makes it look really plain. 


Rear lamps and signals are an improvement, at least they're still amber (had to retrofit 2020s on our car).

1) It's much smoother. This is the biggest improvement by far.

I think this is because they're using the subwoofers for some of the frequencies which would have previously come from the door woofers, but I'm not sure.

author: @ABCDEFG-cj7mr
text:
I know this comment is quite late, but having owned this car for more than a year, I can confidently say that I didn't even notice that the buttons aren't physical at first. They feel like you're actually pressing a button. The tactile feeling is well done, and it works 100% of the time. I actually ended up preferring it over stalks when I got used to it and realized that when driving my sister's Kia occasionally. Almost zero movement with my hand required, super easy to use. The only time where it's bad is if my wheel is upside down, and it takes an extra second to look down, which rarely happens and it's always at slow speeds anyways. 

That said, the car did run into a low-voltage electrical issue at around 16,000 miles. It was taken care of promptly and for free by tesla technicians, but I feel like it shouldn't have happened in the first place. Additionally, I could hear occasional faint rattles after around 20,000 miles for around 20% of my drives (yes, it only happens sometimes. Most drives are completely rattle-free). Not horrible, but annoying when it happens but easily masked with music. Finally, the actual range is only around 260 miles at 80% (quoted 360 miles at full, so around 35 miles less than expected. Not bad, but probably lower due to it learning from my driving habits). 

Overall, he car is honestly amazing and fantastic to drive every day. For its price point, I don't think it gets any better.

author: @zeek3983
text:
For everyone looking forward for a refreshed Model 3 Performance. Possibly called “Model 3 Ludicrous”

Now we know Musk has said that he won’t do a Plaid Model 3 because it would “complicate” the Model 3.

I believe that what he means by this is that putting two Plaid motors in the rear would require so many design changes that it wouldn’t be worth it. However, that doesn’t mean a Model 3 couldn’t get extremely fast with just two motors.

Just look at the trap speeds of a refreshed Model S LR. They are hitting 130+ mph in the 1/4 mile but they really aren’t that much quicker in the 1/4 mile because their 60 foot times are even slower than a Model 3 Performance.

However, if you go back to older Model S Ludicrous cars you can see that those cars could hit sub 1.6 60’ times but they were only trapping about 4 mph more than my Model 3 Performance with weight reductions.

The key here is if you simply combined the top end pulling power of the current Model S LR with the launch modes of the older Model S cars and put it in a Model 3 you would get ridiculous times with almost no complexity added to the Model 3.

The Model 3 doesn’t need three motors to be fast. It doesn’t even need Plaid Carbon wrapped motors to be fast.

It just needs to be able to do a proper launch and be able to hold max power at higher speeds.

If we could turn a 1.60 60’ with a 128+ mph trap speed the Model 3 Ludicrous would probably be able to keep up with a the Corvette E-Ray(10.4) in the 1/4 mile.

I honestly think they might be able to do that with the current 82.1 KWh battery and the two Model S LR motors.

Some of the P90D cars could hit 2.8 second true 0-60 mph times without subtracting rollout. They were hitting plenty of power with less than 10% more battery power than the current Model 3 Performance has.

The current battery is capable of producing plenty of power. You just need motors that can take that power at much higher speeds.

If they do a Model 3 Ludicrous this year I actually think it will be quicker than people are expecting but it won’t have a vastly different batttery or even vastly different motors. I think 10.4 @ 128+ mph is possible and possibly even 0-60 mph in 2.5 seconds. 

As of right now, The absolute quickest acceleration in the Model 3 Performance is achieved when the battery pack temperature is between 125 to 137 degrees Fahrenheit, the State of Charge is 100%, and the motors are as cold as possible. That will give you a “Max Discharge Value” of 629 HP or 462 KW at the battery.

A Model 3 Performance would probably dyno at 538-545 WHP if it was new and fully optimized.

Let us know what kind of times you are expecting if they produce a Tesla Model 3 Ludicrous.

*Notes/Info from Travis Wills*

The car had already been attacked by rust after one winter. This is due to a total lack of rust protection, mixed materials and a far too thin layer of paint.

Now the Danish FDM, the equivalent of the Motormen in Sweden, has gone through the warranty regulations for the most common car brands, where, among other things, rust protection and warranty are one of the parameters.

In the report, which was presented in March 2023, FDM notes that Tesla's warranty is deficient in some respects.

On the one hand, it does not cover all the mechanics connected to the electric drive, which FDM considers to be a consumer requirement. The charging cable, the high current connector and the batteries do not have full warranty coverage.

However, it is the rust protection guarantee that is the worst.

It does not cover paint damage or rust damage, which does not come from the inside.

The warranty terms state: “The Limited Lifetime Body Repair Warranty covers repairs resulting from pitting and deterioration of body parts, but excludes damage caused by rust”.

Just rust through
We Car owners have also noted Tesla's flawed rust protection warranty, which only applies to rusting through, and asked rust protection specialist Thomas Widström about what rusting through means:

“It is extremely rare. It is basically completely impossible for a car owner to prove where the rust has come from," says Thomas Widström.

For those of you who are thinking of giving your Tesla your own good rust protection, however, also have to think twice. This is what it says in the rust protection guarantee:

"Corrosion and paint defects caused due to or as a result of accidents, paint treatment, abuse, negligence, improper maintenance or operation of the vehicle, installation of an accessory, exposure to chemical substances."
The warranty expires
If you treat the undercarriage of your Tesla yourself, it counts as "exposure to chemical substances" and the rust protection then ceases to apply.

This is where Tesla differs from the crowd.

Most other car brands accept that the car owner himself supplements with paint and anti-rust treatments. But in Tesla's case, the warranty then ceases to apply.

Norwegian rust company Funderud Antirust took apart a Model Y to examine the car. According to the film, the rust protection of the best-selling electric car has major flaws, despite a 12-year rust protection guarantee against rusting through. Among other things, exposed areas are not covered by inner screens, the chassis is not galvanized and there is no undercarriage treatment at all. The paintwork is also considerably thinner than on most other cars. Where steel and aluminum meet, galvanic corrosion can also occur.
- We see that there is no PVC wear coating in either the spring tower or the chassis. And we notice the sheet metal joints here. There is no seal in the joints of the plate, which means that salt and water can seep in between.

author: @andrasbiro3007
text:
@kalkal-i5k3c
But that's exactly why it's better then the traditional stalks. If you hold the steering wheel the right way the buttons are always at the same place relative to your thumb.
It's only an issue in tighter roundabouts, where you have to turn the wheel more than 180 degrees. I think that too can be handled with more practice, but I haven't got the chance to try yet.
But of course ideally you want steer-by-wire like the Cybertruck.

As for which button to press, it's easy, the one that's in the direction you want to turn the wheel. If you are turning right, you turn the wheel clockwise (assuming left hand drive), so it's the upper button. Turning left is counter-clockwise, so the lower button.
Once you understand the logic, you can't miss. And it'll become muscle memory very quickly.
The pedals are actually worse, there's no logical reason why the accelerator is right and the brake is left, you have to memorize them. 

Also, Tesla is not the first to go stalkless. Ferrari has been doing it for a long time. They have huge paddle shifters where the stalks would be. 

As for the Yoke, it's not dangerous, just takes some getting used to. Many owners even prefer it instead of the traditional wheel. I would too, if I could afford a new Model S. It looks so much cooler, and doesn't obstruct your view.
And the same rule applies, would be far better with steer-by-wire. Hope all Teslas will get that tech soon.

author: @andrasbiro3007
text:
@RavzzG
Radar is false security. It's extremely noisy, that's why phantom braking is an issue. And that's why Autopilot regularly crashed into stationary obstacles.
Humans drive with "cameras" only, so in any condition where a human can drive, FSD should be able to. Better in fact, as the human eye has a horrible construction, and low sensitivity.

And when conditions are so bad that a human couldn't drive, you probably shouldn't go anywhere anyway.

If snow and dirt prove to be problematic, there are easy solutions. Like the Cybertruck's front bumper camera, that has a dedicated washer.

author: @andrasbiro3007
text:
@wonderboy75
Yes, Elon likes to remove stuff, maybe a bit too much.
I think it's to force his engineers to stop relying on old hardware. It's like when Cortes burned his ships to motivate his soldiers.
It's good leadership, if done right, but in this case hurting the customers.
Probably they expected the software to be ready by the time they deliver the vision-only cars, but got delayed. And there's no changing your mind with hardware, as parts have to be ordered months in advance and production lines can't be changed on the fly either.

Sensors and wipers are no big deal, because you can do everything manually. Maybe it's just because I'm older and learned to drive without fancy gadgets. In the first car I drove you had to manually adjust the air/fuel ratio for cold starts. And shift manually of course.

So, yes, these are issues, but for me the advantages are far bigger. I won't drive anything but a Tesla, if I can avoid it.

FSD is not just Tesla. MAny other brands have promised self-driving and failed to deliver. Google built cars without steering wheels years before Tesla released the first Autopilot. I remember Mercedes and BMW self-driving demos from around 2010 too.
Unfortunately the problem proved to be far far harder than anyone expected.
But Tesla made it very clear from the start that buying FSD is a risk. That's why it was much cheaper at the beginning, and got progressively more expensive as it improved. If things turn out differently, those early buyers could have made a fortune. The estimated value of a robotaxi is $300K.

Currently FSD is good enough to worth the price even without further improvements. Many owners don't drive manually anymore. And one said his wife doesn't let him drive, she feels safer with FSD. And he's not that bad driver.

author: @kalkal-i5k3c
text:
@andrasbiro3007 I'm sorry, but you have no idea what you're talking about.

"You always use the indicator on the side of the direction you're going to turn the steering wheel"?
When I drive in a traffic circle, the steering wheel is upside down. If I want to pull out, I have to turn right (and steer to the right) - so press the left button.

The yoke is extremely dangerous because in a situation where you lose control of the steering wheel and the steering wheel turns uncontrollably fast, it is much more difficult to grab it again because it is asymmetrical.
And the extra time it takes to get the yoke back under control make the difference between life and death.

author: @andrasbiro3007
text:
@kalkal-i5k3c
1. I know what I'm talking about.

2. In a roundabout you still signal the same way. In most cases you don't have to turn the wheel that much. I've tried, I only have to let go of the wheel to use the stalks, so the buttons are actually better in that case.
Tight roundabouts are an issue, but I'm pretty sure it's solvable. I haven't got the chance to practice yet, so I must rely on imagination for now. If you know the wheel is upside down, you just reach for the opposite side, and that's it. It takes practice, but the whole driving thing does. You went to driving school, right?
Of course the ideal solution would be drive-by-wire, like the Cybertruck.

3. Again, you push the button that's in the direction you want to turn. If you want to turn the wheel clockwise, you push the upper button, and the lower one for counter-clockwise turn. Once you know the rule, you won't miss.

4. shouldn't lose control of the steering wheel. I've been driving for almost 30 years, and don't think I've ever lost control.
The only time the yoke is a bit inconvenient is during tight maneuvers at very slow speeds, but then there's no danger.

author: @pauld6967
text:
It is nice that you are happy with the update.

The internal all-around LED lighting "...which you'll notice, especially as you are driving..." sounds like a drawback. I don't want a distraction in the car as I am driving at night.

Deletion of the stalks was definitely a bad move.

That dashboard fabric has got to go. Aftermarket wood will hopefully be available.

The rear display screen is pointless. I have zero interest in back seat passengers being entertained.

As you got low by the headlights, it has circles in the front bumper, so hopefully that isn't an emergency hood release and is Tesla keeping that spot available for ultrasonic sensors once it sinks in that deleting those was a mistake.

Anyway, for me, it seems like the best plan is to go with a 2022 or pre-Highland 2023. Then, after some of these refreshes get into accidents, buy the doors from a salvage yard to have the double-glazed windows. Thus, getting the one important improvement and not sacrificing any of the good things.

Just a shame Tesla cookie-cutter manufactures these. If we had a menu to select the things we like from the pre-Highland version and add what we like feom post-Highland and delete what we don't like from post-Highland,....then we would be truly custom ordering our car.

author: @adjust.clinic
text:
I own a 2019 and 2023 Model 3. Recently, a kid hit my 2019 with his truck, so I have been able to enjoy a rental Audi A5 Sportback. 

I was very excited to drive a comparable German sports sedan. The Audi I think is around $55K, so more expensive. And the Audi is only 100lbs lighter. It's got a nice interior. 

But the Model 3 is a far, far sportier car. Compared to the Audi, the Tesla has got direct steering feel. Its handling is flat, neutral, and completely controllable. Throttle response is instant, and has enough power to deliver whatever you need to do. 

The Audi is awkward. You step on the gas pedal, and you wait a second as it feels like it's bogged down, then without warning, the turbo kicks in for angry acceleration, even if you don't want it. In the most "dynamic" setting, the car is numb, and it reminds me of my 1981 Buick Regal I had in high school. You'll never upset the chassis in the Audi because it's so underpowered. And, it's no fun to drive. 

To add insult: I can't figure out how to refuel the Audi from my house. I have to stop at gas stations. 

I can't wait to get my 2019 Model 3 back from the shop...

author: @davwvid
text:
oh no, blinkers as buttons is a v bad idea. There were where they were in most cars because it was practical to turn the steering wheel and on the way just nudge the stalk in a direction the wheel is turning with your finger. It was obvious and intuitive. With buttons you need to remember that right is up, left is down, and if the wheel is already turned 90 deg anticlockwise (on a roundabout for example), suddenly right blinker is the button on the left. How does that make any sense? Not to mention that you don't just turn the wheel holding your hands in the same spot, you kinda always default into holding the wheel more or less on the same level, in the middle. Meaning, at 90 deg, the buttons are at the bottom of the steering wheel, and you need to reach down to them (and figure out that the right blinker is on the left actually lol). I get that this wasn't a consideration in the US because you guys have like 10 roundabouts in total, but in EU and basically anywhere else they are everywhere, in different sizes, different angles of exit etc, so muscle memory won't help here, and IMO, even if it did, it still seems dangerous or inconvinient at best.

This is objectively, the worst design choice in a car I've seen in a while. And I don't understand why they did it to begin with. I see 0 benefits. If it was for minimalism, I can't see how a button in front of you is more minimalistic than a thing sticking out behind the wheel that you can't see for most of the time, because, well, its behind the wheel :D
Just innovation for the sake of innovation. The worst kind.

Thankfully in EU this won't be allowed (right?)

Also, where is the horn button? I don't see anything in the middle... is it in the menus or what happened? (that was btw already played around with in Renault cars from around 2010s. Everyone hated that they moved the horn from the middle, to a stalk in front of the blinkers. Why? Who knows, they are french, nobody understands them anyway).

Smartphones were an offshoot of Canadian company Research In Motion who showed the value of an always connected mobile device with data.  Before that it was Nokia and Motorola who dominated the field.  Now we just take it for granted.

Many cutting edge tech companies have their roots in university settings.

text:

University of Waterloo has a long Computer Science history and was a part of those early connected learning institutions. 
We were (may still be?) The only North American university with a Faculty of Mathematics where you get a BMath degree and an extensive computer science history.  Others give a BScience in Mathematics. 
Canadian banks rolled out nationwide ATMs quicker as we have national banks rather than predominantly regional US banking.
Connected mobile devices were a product of Canadian company Research In Motion and BlackBerrys. 
But... we Canadians are quieter about our successes.  Humility comes with 11 months of winter 😉
